text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Hundreds of thousands take part in anti-German protests in Tehran but Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel speaks out against breaking off diplomatic relations.
- Oskar Lafontaine, leader of opposition Social Democrats (SPD), says this week's meeting with government on tax reform must bring a breakthrough.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl says tax burden for businesses must be reduced.
- Conflict over trade union proposals for a 32-hour working week instensifies.
HANDELSBLATT
- Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU), junior partners in Kohl's government, want smaller cut in top rate of income tax than planned.
- Pension contributions to go below 20 percent under deal hammered out within coalition.
- Kohl sees signs of economic upturn in early part of this year.
- Six leading economic research institutes believe Germany will miss the budget deficit target for European monetary union (EMU), the Berliner Zeitung newspaper says.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber sticks to criticism of Bonn government and Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
- Kohl singles out tax reform plans as key to upturn in German economy.
- Number of homes built in Germany declined slightly in 1996 compared to the previous year, Construction Minister Klaus Toepfer says.
DIE WELT
- Kinkel says it is time to reassess relations with Iran.
- Hanover trade fair opens its doors with 7,259 exhibitors from 69 countries.
- Employers want to block union plan for 32-hour week, even if industrial conflict is required.
